decks.title: International Organisations — Part 1: Why They Matter and How the UN Works
goals: Explain why states need international organisations
Trace the evolution of the UN from the League of Nations
Describe the six principal organs and the specialised agencies
Apply the voting rules of the Security Council

slides.heading: International Organisations
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why states create organisations, and how the **United Nations** is built.

nodes.label: From the League to the UN

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why international organisations, from the League to the UN, aims, six principal organs, Security Council voting, specialised agencies
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Think about an outbreak of a new disease, a war on a border, or a dispute over trade. None of these stops at a national boundary. In this chapter we ask why states build international organisations, how the United Nations came to be, and how its main parts work. In the second part we look at calls for reform, India's place in that debate, and other important organisations.

slides.heading: Why international organisations?
slides.body_md: Some problems are too big for any one state.

headers: Why one state cannot solve it alone
rows: Early warning and common health standards
A forum for talks and peacekeeping
Rules must be the same for all
Agreed rules and a place to settle disputes

visual.alt: Table of four shared problems (epidemics, war, trade and money, climate) with why one state cannot solve each alone and how an international organisation helps

slides.narration: Look at the table. Diseases spread quickly across borders. Wars begin when states distrust each other. Trade needs rules that are the same for everybody. Pollution does not respect boundaries. In each case, a body where states meet regularly, share information and agree on rules makes cooperation easier and cheaper. That is the basic reason why international organisations exist.

slides.heading: Not a world government
bullets: Created by **states**, through agreement; works through their **consent**.
Has **no army of its own**; depends on members for troops and money.
Helps states **talk, cooperate and settle disputes**, but cannot guarantee peace.
slides.narration: A common mistake is to think of the United Nations as a world government. It is not. States create it, pay for it and send it soldiers when they choose. It cannot arrest leaders or abolish war. What it can do is give every state a place to talk, a set of rules and a way to act together when they agree.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: True or false? The United Nations is a world government above all sovereign states.
slides.narration: Pause and decide. Remember who creates the organisation and whose consent it needs.

slides.heading: From the League to the UN

visual.alt: Flow from the League of Nations in 1920, through the Second World War and the Atlantic Charter of 1941, to the Charter signed at San Francisco in June 1945 and the UN beginning on 24 October 1945
visual.caption: From the League to the UN

slides.narration: The League of Nations began work in 1920 after the First World War, but it could not stop the Second World War. During that war the allies planned a stronger body. The Atlantic Charter of 1941 set out shared aims. In June 1945 the Charter was signed at San Francisco, and the United Nations came into existence on the twenty fourth of October 1945 with fifty one members.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ordering events
slides.body_md: Arrange five events in order without memorising every date.
bullets: Step 1 — Anchor each event to a **war or era**: First World War, Second World War, Cold War, after the Cold War.
Step 2 — Place the League first and the UN at the end of the Second World War.
Step 3 — Cold War institutions such as the **IAEA** come next; the **WTO** comes after the Cold War.

rows: End of the Second World War
Atoms for peace, Cold War years

visual.alt: Chronology table: League of Nations 1920, Atlantic Charter 1941, UN Charter and UN 1945, IAEA 1957, WTO 1995
visual.caption: Anchor each event to a war or era before you memorise the year.

slides.narration: Chronology questions become easy if you hang each event on a big peg. The League follows the First World War. The Atlantic Charter and the UN belong to the Second World War. The IAEA, set up in 1957, belongs to the Cold War years. The WTO, from 1995, comes after the Cold War. Use the eras first, then the years.

slides.heading: Aims of the UN

nodes.label: Cooperate on economic, social and humanitarian problems

visual.alt: Flow listing the aims of the UN: peace and security, friendly relations, cooperation on economic, social and humanitarian problems, and respect for human rights
visual.caption: Aims of the UN (in brief)

slides.narration: The Charter gives the UN a few broad aims. The first is to keep international peace and security. Others are to develop friendly relations among nations, to cooperate in solving economic, social and humanitarian problems, and to promote respect for human rights. Every organ we study next serves one or more of these aims.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: On which date did the United Nations come into existence?
slides.narration: Think about the difference between signing the Charter and the organisation actually beginning.

visual.caption: The six principal organs set up by the Charter.

slides.narration: The Charter set up six principal organs. Above the Charter in this diagram are the General Assembly, the Security Council and the Economic and Social Council. Below are the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council. The Trusteeship Council is drawn with a dashed line because it suspended its work in 1994, when the last trust territory became independent.

slides.heading: The General Assembly

rows: One state, one vote; important questions need a two-thirds majority
Debates world issues, approves the budget, elects non-permanent Council members

visual.alt: Table on the General Assembly: all member states, one state one vote, debates issues, approves the budget, elects non-permanent members, resolutions mostly recommendations

slides.narration: The General Assembly is the one place where every member sits. Each state has one vote, whether it is large or small, rich or poor. It debates world issues, approves the budget and elects the non permanent members of the Security Council. Most of its resolutions are recommendations, which carry moral and political weight but are not orders.

visual.caption: The Security Council at a glance.

slides.narration: The Security Council has fifteen members. Five are permanent: the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Russia and China. Each of them holds a veto. The other ten are elected by the General Assembly for two year terms, five each year. A substantive decision needs at least nine votes in favour and no vote against from a permanent member.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: will the resolution pass?
slides.body_md: Apply two tests to each imagined vote.
bullets: Test 1 — Are there at least **9** votes in favour?
Test 2 — Did any **permanent member vote no**? If yes, it is a veto.
An **abstention** by a permanent member is not treated as a veto.

visual.alt: Worked example table of three imagined votes in a 15-member Council: A has 11 yes but a permanent member votes no, so it is not adopted; B has 9 yes and no permanent no, so it is adopted; C has only 8 yes, 1 short of nine, so it is not adopted
visual.caption: Imagined votes. Two tests: at least nine yes, and no permanent member voting no.

slides.narration: Let us apply the rules. Resolution A has eleven votes in favour, but a permanent member voted against, so it fails. Resolution B has exactly nine votes in favour and no permanent member voted no, so it passes. Resolution C has eight votes in favour and nobody voted no, but it is still one vote short of nine, so it fails.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: What is the minimum number of votes in favour that a substantive resolution needs?
slides.narration: Use the rule from the worked example and remember the size of the Council.

slides.heading: The other principal organs

rows: Coordinates economic, social and humanitarian work with the agencies
Settles legal disputes between states; advisory opinions
Daily administration; headed by the Secretary-General
Staff serve the UN, not their own states

visual.alt: Table of four principal organs: ECOSOC coordinates economic and social work, the ICJ settles legal disputes at The Hague, the Secretariat runs daily administration under the Secretary-General, and the Trusteeship Council suspended work in 1994

slides.narration: The Economic and Social Council coordinates work on economic and social questions and links the UN with its specialised agencies. The International Court of Justice at The Hague settles legal disputes between states. The Secretariat, headed by the Secretary General, runs the daily work. The Trusteeship Council once supervised trust territories and has been inactive since 1994.

slides.heading: Specialised agencies

visual.alt: Table of four specialised agencies and their fields: WHO health, ILO labour, FAO food and farming, UNESCO education, science and culture
visual.caption: Agencies are separate bodies linked to the UN and coordinated through ECOSOC.

slides.narration: Around the principal organs is a family of specialised agencies. Each is a separate organisation with its own members and budget, linked to the UN by agreement. The World Health Organization works on health, the International Labour Organization on workers, the Food and Agriculture Organization on food and farming, and UNESCO on education, science and culture.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: Which principal organ does an official who runs the daily administration of the UN work for?
slides.narration: Think about which organ is made up of staff rather than member states.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Cross-border problems need cooperation; a forum lowers suspicion
After the League failed; UN begins 24 October 1945 with 51 members
Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, ICJ, Secretariat, Trusteeship Council
15 members; five permanent with a veto; nine votes for a decision

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: why organisations, birth of the UN, the six principal organs, and Security Council voting

slides.narration: To sum up. Shared problems push states to cooperate through organisations. The UN replaced the failed League in 1945 with fifty one members. It has six principal organs, of which the Trusteeship Council is now inactive. The Security Council has fifteen members, five permanent with a veto, and needs nine votes for a decision.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Do not call the UN a **world government**: it works through member states.
Write the full **six** organs; mention that the Trusteeship Council is **inactive since 1994**.
For voting questions, apply **two tests**: nine votes, and no permanent member voting no.
Assembly = **one state, one vote**; IMF and World Bank = **weighted** votes.
Marks: 2 marks = two points; 3 marks = three points on clear bases; 5 marks = five organs or points.
slides.narration: A few tips. Never describe the UN as a world government. When asked for the principal organs, give all six and note that the Trusteeship Council is inactive. For voting questions, check both conditions: nine votes and no veto. Do not mix up the equal vote in the General Assembly with the weighted votes in the financial institutions. Match the number of points to the marks.

decks.title: International Organisations — Part 2: Reform, India and Other Organisations
goals: Explain why the UN needs reform after the Cold War and the two kinds of reform
Evaluate proposals for Security Council reform, including the veto
Describe India's position on UN reform, with arguments and objections
State the roles of the IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch

slides.heading: Reform, India and other organisations
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why the UN is being asked to **change**, where **India** stands, and the work of **other organisations**.

nodes.label: Why reform after the Cold War

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why reform after the Cold War, two kinds of reform, criteria and the veto debate, India and UN reform, IMF, World Bank, WTO and IAEA, and human rights NGOs
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: The UN of 1945 was built for the world of 1945. Since then, the number of states has grown nearly fourfold, the Cold War has ended and new problems have appeared. In this part we look at why reform is demanded, what kinds of reform are proposed, India's claim to a permanent seat, and the work of other important organisations.

slides.heading: Why reform after the Cold War?

rows: 193 members, many from Asia, Africa and Latin America
Cold War over; new powers and new economies
Also terrorism, civil wars, climate, disease
Permanent five chosen by the winners of the war

visual.alt: Table comparing 1945 and now: 51 against 193 members, Cold War against a changed world, war between states against new threats, and the same permanent five

slides.narration: Compare 1945 with today. The UN began with fifty one members; today it has one hundred and ninety three, many from Asia, Africa and Latin America. The Cold War is over, new economies have risen, and threats now include terrorism, civil wars, climate change and disease. Yet the same five permanent members sit on the Security Council. This gap is the heart of the reform debate.

slides.heading: Two kinds of reform

rows: How the UN is organised and decides
Changing Security Council membership or the veto
Which issues the UN should deal with

visual.alt: Table of the two kinds of UN reform: structures and processes, for example Security Council membership and the veto; and jurisdiction, for example terrorism, development and human rights

slides.narration: Reform is discussed under two heads. The first is reform of structures and processes: how the UN is organised and how it decides, for example who sits on the Security Council and whether the veto should change. The second is jurisdiction: which issues the UN should take up, such as terrorism, development or human rights.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: Name the two broad parts of the UN reform debate.
slides.narration: One part is about how the UN is organised; the other is about what it deals with.

slides.heading: Criteria for new permanent members

rows: Substantial contributor to the UN budget

visual.alt: Table of six proposed criteria for new permanent members: economic power, military power, budget contribution, large population, democracy and human rights, regional and cultural diversity
visual.caption: Proposals made in the reform debate; no criterion has been formally adopted.

slides.narration: If new permanent members are added, who should they be? Proposals in the debate include being a major economic or military power, contributing substantially to the UN budget, having a large population, respecting democracy and human rights, and adding to the regional and cultural diversity of the Council. None of these has been formally adopted, and each is disputed.

slides.heading: The veto debate

rows: Keeps major powers inside the UN
Lets one state block the will of the majority
Decisions backed by the strong are easier to enforce
Leaves the Council silent in some crises
Avoids the fate of the League

visual.alt: Table of arguments to keep the veto (keeps major powers in, easier enforcement, avoids the League's fate) and to limit it (one state blocks the majority, Council silent in crises, reflects 1945)

slides.narration: The veto is the most argued feature of the Council. Supporters say it keeps the major powers inside the organisation and makes decisions easier to enforce, avoiding the fate of the League. Critics say it lets one state block the wishes of the majority and reflects the power balance of 1945. Changing it would itself need the agreement of the permanent members.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: weighing a candidate
slides.body_md: Rate an imagined state against the proposed criteria.
bullets: Step 1 — List each criterion and the evidence for the state.
Step 2 — Mark **yes, partly or no**.
Step 3 — **Weigh** them: some states stress regional balance, others economic weight.
Step 4 — Conclude with reasons, not just a count of ticks.

rows: Its region already has a permanent member

visual.alt: Worked example table rating an imagined state, Varunadesh, against five criteria: economic power yes, budget contribution yes, population partly, democracy yes, regional balance no
visual.caption: Imagined state. Weigh the criteria; do not just count ticks.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined state, Varunadesh. It has a large economy, pays a lot into the UN budget and holds regular elections. Its population is moderate, and its region already has a permanent member. A good answer does not just count ticks. It explains which criteria matter more and why, and admits that other states may weigh them differently.

slides.heading: India and UN reform

rows: One of the two most populous countries and the largest democracy
Large, growing economy; regular UN contributions
Doubt whether one state can speak for a whole region
Some states oppose any new permanent seats

visual.alt: Table of arguments made for India's permanent seat (population and democracy, peacekeeping, economy and contributions, voice for developing countries) and objections raised by some states (nuclear weapons, disputes with neighbours, regional representation, opposition to new permanent seats)
visual.caption: Stated as the views of different states, not as verdicts.

slides.narration: India supports a more representative Security Council and seeks a permanent seat. Arguments made for it include its very large population and democracy, its long record in peacekeeping, its growing economy and its regular contributions. India works with Brazil, Germany and Japan, who seek seats too. Some states raise objections, and some oppose any new permanent seats, so the debate continues.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: Which reason is most consistent with the view of states that oppose any new permanent members?
slides.narration: Think about what a new permanent seat, especially with a veto, would do to equality among members.

slides.heading: The UN and a dominant power
bullets: After the Cold War, one power had unmatched military and economic strength.
A **large budget share** and a **veto** give a powerful member leverage.
Yet the UN remains the main **forum where all states can speak**, and powers often seek its approval.
slides.narration: After the Cold War, some observers worried that a single dominant power could bend the UN to its will, since it paid a large share of the budget and held a veto. Others pointed out that even a powerful state values the legitimacy the UN provides. For smaller states, the UN remains the main place where their voice can be heard.

slides.heading: Other international organisations

rows: Global financial system; help in payments crises
Rules of world trade; trade disputes

visual.alt: Table of the IMF and World Bank (planned at Bretton Woods in 1944), the WTO (1995, after GATT) and the IAEA (1957) with their main roles

slides.narration: Beyond the principal organs, four organisations appear often in your syllabus. The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were planned at Bretton Woods in 1944. The World Trade Organization was set up in 1995, following the earlier GATT framework. The International Atomic Energy Agency was set up in 1957 to promote peaceful nuclear energy.

slides.heading: IMF and World Bank

rows: Short-term loans in payments crises; policy advice
Loans and grants for roads, schools, health, farming
Projects and conditions shaped by rich members

visual.alt: Comparison table of the IMF and World Bank: focus, typical help, weighted voting, and common criticisms

slides.narration: The IMF looks after the stability of the global financial system and lends to countries in a payments crisis, often with conditions. The World Bank finances long term development such as roads, schools and health. In both, votes are weighted by each member's financial contribution, so rich members have more say. This is a common criticism from developing countries.

slides.heading: WTO and IAEA

rows: Developing states say big economies set the agenda
Inspections need the consent of states

visual.alt: Comparison table of the WTO (trade rules, dispute settlement, debate about big economies) and the IAEA (peaceful nuclear energy, inspections, need for consent)

slides.narration: The World Trade Organization sets the rules of international trade and settles trade disputes. Developing countries often say that big economies set its agenda. The International Atomic Energy Agency helps countries use nuclear technology for power, medicine and farming, and its inspectors check that nuclear material is not turned into weapons.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which organisation?
slides.body_md: Match each imagined need to the right organisation.
bullets: Step 1 — Identify the **field**: money, development, trade, nuclear or rights.
Step 2 — Recall the organisation for that field.
Step 3 — Give a one-line reason.

rows: Reserves cover only one month of imports
Short-term help in a payments crisis
Loan for hill roads and village schools
A partner breaks agreed tariff rules
Proof that a reactor is peaceful
Amnesty International or Human Rights Watch

visual.alt: Worked example table matching five imagined needs to the IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA and human rights NGOs, with reasons
visual.caption: Imagined needs. Match the problem to the field of the organisation.

slides.narration: Here are five imagined needs. A country whose reserves cover only a month of imports goes to the IMF. One that wants a loan for hill roads goes to the World Bank. A dispute over tariff rules goes to the WTO. Proof that a reactor is peaceful comes from the IAEA. Journalists held without trial attract the attention of human rights NGOs.

slides.heading: Human rights NGOs

rows: Prisoners of conscience, torture, death penalty
Child soldiers, landmines, abuses in conflicts
No power to enforce; influence through publicity
No power to enforce; influence through publicity

visual.alt: Comparison table of Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch: both NGOs, their methods, examples of their concerns, and their lack of enforcement power

slides.narration: Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are not part of the UN and are not run by governments. They are non governmental organisations. They investigate abuses, publish reports, work with the media and lobby governments. They cannot enforce anything, but their publicity can put strong pressure on governments to change.

slides.heading: Quick check
slides.body_md: Which organisation best fits this description: an NGO that researches abuses such as the use of child soldiers and lobbies governments?
slides.narration: Look for the clue that it is a non governmental organisation based in New York.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Membership and the world changed; the permanent five did not
Seeks a permanent seat; works with Brazil, Germany and Japan; faces objections
IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA; NGOs Amnesty and HRW

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: why reform, two kinds of reform, India's claim, and other organisations

slides.narration: To sum up. The world has changed since 1945 but the permanent five have not, so reform is demanded in structures and in jurisdiction. Proposals for new permanent members and the veto are disputed. India seeks a permanent seat and faces objections from some states. The IMF, World Bank, WTO and IAEA have specialised roles, while NGOs work through publicity.

slides.heading: Exam tips

sections.heading: 1. Why international organisations?
sections.body_md:
An **international organisation** is a body set up by **states, through agreement**, to help them cooperate. It is **not a world government**: it acts through the consent of its members and has no army of its own.

**Why needed:**
- Many problems (epidemics, conflict, trade, climate) **cross borders**.
- A permanent body gives **rules, information and a meeting place**, which lowers distrust and the cost of each negotiation.
- It offers **smaller states a voice**.

They cannot abolish war, but they make cooperation and peaceful settlement more likely.

key_terms.definition_md: A body created by agreement among states to help them cooperate on shared problems.
A state with supreme authority over its own territory, which joins organisations by its own choice.

sections.heading: 2. Evolution of the UN
sections.body_md:
- The **League of Nations** (1920) was formed after the First World War but failed to prevent the Second.
- During that war the allies planned a new body; the **Atlantic Charter** (1941) set out common aims.
- The **UN Charter** was signed at the **San Francisco** conference in **June 1945**.
- The UN came into existence on **24 October 1945** (UN Day) with **51** members; today it has **193**.
- **India** was one of the founding members.

**Aims:** maintain international peace and security; develop friendly relations among nations; cooperate on economic, social and humanitarian problems; promote human rights.

sections.heading: 3. Principal organs and specialised agencies
sections.body_md:
1. **General Assembly:** all members; **one state, one vote**; debates, budget, elections; resolutions mostly **recommendations**.
2. **Security Council:** **15 members**: **5 permanent** (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) with a **veto**, **10 non-permanent** elected by the Assembly for **two-year terms** (five each year). A substantive decision needs **9 votes** and **no negative vote** by a permanent member; an abstention is not a veto.
3. **Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC):** economic and social cooperation; coordinates specialised agencies.
4. **International Court of Justice:** at **The Hague**; legal disputes between states; advisory opinions.
5. **Secretariat:** administration; headed by the **Secretary-General**, appointed by the Assembly on the Council's recommendation.
6. **Trusteeship Council:** supervised trust territories; **suspended operations in 1994**.

**Specialised agencies** (WHO, ILO, FAO, UNESCO and others) are separate organisations linked to the UN and coordinated through ECOSOC.

key_terms.definition_md: The power of each permanent member to block a substantive Security Council decision by voting against it.
An autonomous organisation working in one field, linked to the UN by agreement.

sections.heading: 4. Reform of the UN after the Cold War
sections.body_md:
**Why:** membership has grown from 51 to 193; the Cold War is over; new powers and new threats (terrorism, civil wars, climate, disease) have emerged; but the **permanent five** remain those of 1945.

**Two kinds of reform:**
- **Structures and processes:** membership of the Security Council, the veto, working methods.
- **Jurisdiction:** which issues the UN should take up.

**Proposed criteria for new permanent members** (debated, none adopted): major economic power; major military power; substantial budget contribution; large population; respect for democracy and human rights; adding regional and cultural diversity.

**The veto:** supporters say it keeps great powers committed and makes action enforceable; critics call it undemocratic and outdated. Changing the Charter needs the agreement of the permanent members.

**A dominant power:** after the Cold War, concern grew that one powerful member could shape the UN through its budget share and veto; yet the UN remains the main forum for all states.

sections.heading: 5. India and UN reform
sections.body_md:
India supports a **stronger, more representative UN** with an **expanded Security Council** in both categories, and seeks a **permanent seat**. It works with **Brazil, Germany and Japan** (the G4), which also seek seats.

**Grounds put forward:** one of the two most populous countries and the largest democracy; long participation in **UN peacekeeping**; a large and growing economy and regular contributions; a voice for developing countries; it has served as an **elected member several times** (most recently 2021–22).

**Objections raised by some states:** possession of nuclear weapons; disputes with neighbours; doubts about regional representation; and a group of states that opposes **any** new permanent seats and prefers more elected seats.

These are positions held by different states; examiners expect both sides.

sections.heading: 6. Other international organisations
sections.body_md:
- **IMF:** planned at **Bretton Woods (1944)**; oversees the international financial system, advises on policy and lends in **payments crises**; votes weighted by **quota**.
- **World Bank:** also from Bretton Woods; loans and grants for **development** (infrastructure, education, health, agriculture, environment, governance); criticised for conditions.
- **WTO:** set up in **1995** as the successor to **GATT (1948)**; rules of world trade and **dispute settlement**; developing countries say major economies dominate.
- **IAEA:** set up in **1957**; promotes **peaceful nuclear energy** and runs **safeguard inspections**.
- **Amnesty International:** an **NGO** that researches abuses, publishes reports and campaigns for human rights.
- **Human Rights Watch:** an **NGO** based in New York; investigation, media and lobbying, for example against **child soldiers and landmines**.

NGOs have **no enforcement power**; their influence comes from publicity.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling the UN a world government, or saying it has its own army.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes an **international organisation** such as the UN?

options.text_md: A world government whose orders every citizen must obey directly
A body created by states, through agreement, to help them cooperate on shared problems
A private company that trades across many countries
A military alliance that one country controls

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A body created by states, through agreement, to help them cooperate on shared problems. International organisations are set up by member states and work through their consent; they are not a world government above states. A trading company is a private firm, and an alliance run by one country is not a cooperative body of equals.

questions.stem_md: A new virus spreads from one imagined country, Tamralipti, to its neighbours within weeks. Why is an international organisation especially useful in such a case?

options.text_md: Because an international organisation can arrest the officials of Tamralipti
Because each neighbour can solve the problem better by closing all contact with the world permanently
Because international organisations exist only to deal with diseases
The problem crosses borders, so no single state can tackle it alone; a common body helps share information and coordinate action

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The problem crosses borders, so no single state can tackle it alone; a common body helps share information and coordinate action. Cross-border problems such as epidemics need cooperation, and an international body lowers the cost of sharing information and coordinating action. Such bodies cannot arrest a state's officials, permanent isolation is not a solution, and they deal with many issues, not only health.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a realistic expectation from an international organisation like the UN?

options.text_md: It can help states discuss disputes and reach peaceful solutions, though it cannot always prevent war
It can abolish all wars between states for ever
It can take over the government of any member that breaks a rule
It can make every member state agree on every issue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It can help states discuss disputes and reach peaceful solutions, though it cannot always prevent war. The UN is a forum where states negotiate and cooperate; its success depends on members. It cannot guarantee that wars will never happen, cannot replace a member's government at will, and cannot force agreement on every issue.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** States often find it easier to cooperate through an international organisation than one by one.

**Reason (R):** An international organisation provides rules, information and a regular meeting place, which reduce suspicion and the cost of each new negotiation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a standing body with agreed procedures and shared information makes cooperation cheaper and more predictable than repeated one-to-one bargaining.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The United Nations is a world government that stands above all sovereign states.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The UN is an organisation of sovereign states; it acts through the consent and cooperation of its members and has no army or police of its own that it can use at will.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why states in today's world need international organisations.
questions.solution_md: One reason about cross-border problems and one about the forum and rules that such a body provides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Many problems, such as **epidemics, climate change and terrorism**, cross borders and need **joint action** by many states.
2. A permanent body offers **rules, information and a forum**, so states can settle differences by **talking rather than fighting**.

marking_scheme.step: Forum and rules for peaceful discussion

questions.stem_md: An imagined student, Rehana, argues in a school debate: "International organisations are useless, because powerful states do what they want anyway." Give three points with which you could reply to her.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct counter-points: shared rules benefit all, voice for weaker states, conflict reduction and practical achievements; a balanced reply may admit the limits she points to.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Even powerful states **gain from rules**: trade, air travel, postal links and health alerts all depend on agreed international standards.
2. Organisations give **smaller states a voice** and a place to raise complaints that would otherwise be ignored.
3. They **lower the chance of conflict** by keeping states talking, and their record in areas such as **peacekeeping, refugees and disease control** shows real results, even if they cannot stop every war.

Voice and forum for smaller states

questions.stem_md: Which of the following helps explain why an international organisation can make cooperation easier among states that distrust each other?

options.text_md: It forces the strongest member to give up its army
It lets each member ignore any agreement it dislikes without consequence
It gives all members the same information and a fixed set of procedures for decisions
It replaces national parliaments in making laws

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It gives all members the same information and a fixed set of procedures for decisions. Shared information and agreed procedures reduce suspicion. No organisation disarms its strongest member, membership does carry obligations, and it does not replace national parliaments.

questions.stem_md: The United Nations came into existence on

options.text_md: 26 June 1945
1 January 1942
24 October 1945
10 January 1920

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 24 October 1945. The UN Charter was signed at San Francisco in June 1945, and the organisation came into existence on 24 October 1945, now observed as UN Day. 1942 is the year of the declaration by the wartime allies, and 1920 the year the League of Nations began work.

questions.stem_md: Which organisation was the predecessor of the United Nations, set up after the First World War?

options.text_md: The League of Nations
The World Trade Organization
The Non-Aligned Movement
The International Atomic Energy Agency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The League of Nations. The League of Nations was created after the First World War; its failure to prevent the Second World War led to the creation of the UN. The WTO (1995), NAM (1961) and IAEA (1957) all came later.

questions.stem_md: How many states were founding (original) members of the United Nations in 1945?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 51. The UN began with 51 member states. 193 is its present membership, and 15 is the size of the Security Council.

questions.stem_md: In the UN General Assembly,

options.text_md: votes are weighted by each member's population
every member state has one vote, whatever its size or wealth
only the five permanent members can vote
votes are weighted by each member's financial contribution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** every member state has one vote, whatever its size or wealth. The General Assembly works on the principle of one state, one vote. Weighted voting by money is a feature of the IMF and World Bank, not the Assembly, and the permanent members matter in the Security Council, not here.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Japan. The five permanent members are the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China. Japan has been elected a non-permanent member many times but has no permanent seat.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the **veto** in the UN Security Council?

options.text_md: The right of any Council member to leave the meeting
A negative vote by any one permanent member that stops a substantive decision, even if the others support it
The power of the General Assembly to overrule the Security Council
The right of the Secretary-General to cancel a resolution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A negative vote by any one permanent member that stops a substantive decision, even if the others support it. Each of the five permanent members can block a substantive resolution by voting against it. Non-permanent members have no such power, the Assembly cannot overrule the Council on security matters, and the Secretary-General has no veto.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined states, Aranya and Meghpur, disagree over where their sea boundary lies and both agree to let a UN body decide according to international law. Which principal organ will hear the case?

options.text_md: The Economic and Social Council
The Trusteeship Council
The International Court of Justice
The Secretariat

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The International Court of Justice. Legal disputes between states that accept its jurisdiction go to the International Court of Justice at The Hague. ECOSOC deals with economic and social matters, the Trusteeship Council has been inactive since 1994, and the Secretariat is the administrative staff.

questions.stem_md: Why has the Trusteeship Council suspended its operations since 1994?

options.text_md: It was merged into the Security Council
Its members could not agree on a chairperson
It was replaced by the World Trade Organization
The last trust territory became independent, so it had no territories left to supervise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The last trust territory became independent, so it had no territories left to supervise. The Council supervised territories placed under trusteeship; when the last of them (Palau) became independent in 1994, it suspended operations. It was not merged with the Security Council and has nothing to do with the WTO.

questions.stem_md: A UN official based in New York prepares reports, organises conferences and carries out the day-to-day administration of the organisation. Which principal organ does this official work for?

options.text_md: The General Assembly
The International Court of Justice
The Security Council
The Secretariat

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Secretariat. The Secretariat, headed by the Secretary-General, runs the daily work of the UN. The Assembly and the Council are bodies of member states, and the ICJ is a court.

questions.stem_md: A UN body coordinates the work of agencies dealing with health, education, labour and development, and discusses reports on poverty. Which principal organ is this?

options.text_md: The Security Council
The International Court of Justice
The Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)
The Trusteeship Council

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). ECOSOC coordinates the economic, social and related work of the UN and its specialised agencies. The Security Council deals with peace and security, the ICJ with legal disputes, and the Trusteeship Council with trust territories.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country asks a UN specialised agency for help to set fair standards for factory working hours and the safety of workers. Which agency deals with such matters?

options.text_md: The World Health Organization (WHO)
The International Labour Organization (ILO)
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The International Labour Organization (ILO). Labour standards and workers' rights are the field of the ILO. WHO deals with health, FAO with food and farming, and the IAEA with nuclear energy.

questions.stem_md: The ten non-permanent members of the Security Council are

options.text_md: elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms
appointed by the five permanent members for life
chosen by the Secretary-General every five years
selected by lottery among all member states each year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. The General Assembly elects the ten non-permanent members for two-year terms, five each year. They are not appointed by the permanent members or the Secretary-General, and there is no lottery.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A resolution of the Security Council can pass even if one permanent member abstains.

**Reason (R):** The non-permanent members of the Security Council are elected for two-year terms.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. In practice an abstention by a permanent member is not treated as a veto, so the resolution can pass with nine votes in favour. R is a true fact about elected members, but it does not explain why an abstention is not a veto.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The United Nations was set up after the Second World War.

**Reason (R):** The League of Nations, set up after the First World War, had failed to prevent another world war.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the failure of the League to keep peace led the wartime allies to plan a stronger organisation, the UN, in 1945.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every resolution of the General Assembly is legally binding on all member states.

**Reason (R):** In the General Assembly each member state has one vote.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: most General Assembly resolutions are recommendations; decisions of the Security Council on peace and security are the ones members have agreed to carry out. R is true: the Assembly follows one state, one vote.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Trusteeship Council is one of the six principal organs of the UN, although it suspended its operations in 1994.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Charter lists six principal organs, including the Trusteeship Council; it stopped regular work in 1994 after the last trust territory became independent.

questions.stem_md: The headquarters of the United Nations is in ___, and the International Court of Justice sits at ___.
questions.solution_md: The UN headquarters is in New York; the ICJ sits at The Hague in the Netherlands.

questions.stem_md: Match each principal organ of the UN with its main work.

options.text_md: General Assembly
Security Council
International Court of Justice
Secretariat

match_right.text_md: Primary responsibility for international peace and security
Day-to-day administration, headed by the Secretary-General
All members discuss world issues and pass recommendations, one state one vote

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Assembly: forum of all members; Council: peace and security; ICJ: legal disputes; Secretariat: administration.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events on the road to and beyond the founding of the UN in chronological order.

options.text_md: The UN Charter is signed at the San Francisco conference
The League of Nations begins work after the First World War
The World Trade Organization replaces the GATT framework
The International Atomic Energy Agency is set up
The Atlantic Charter is announced by the leaders of the USA and the UK

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). League of Nations (1920) → Atlantic Charter (1941) → UN Charter signed (June 1945) → IAEA (1957) → WTO (1995).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: The Security Council has 15 members. What is the minimum number of votes in favour that a substantive resolution needs (provided no permanent member votes against it)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A substantive decision needs the affirmative votes of nine of the fifteen members.
Step 2: So at least 9 votes, with no negative vote from a permanent member.

questions.stem_md: The Security Council has 10 non-permanent members, each elected for a two-year term, with the terms staggered. How many non-permanent members does the General Assembly elect in a normal year?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ten seats, each held for two years, are filled in two equal halves.
Step 2: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 members each year.

questions.stem_md: Name any four principal organs of the United Nations.
questions.solution_md: Half a mark for each correct organ, up to four.

answer.model_answer_md: Any four of: the **General Assembly**, the **Security Council**, the **Economic and Social Council**, the **International Court of Justice**, the **Secretariat** and the **Trusteeship Council**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the composition of the UN Security Council.
questions.solution_md: State the total, the permanent five with their veto, and the ten elected members with their term.

answer.model_answer_md: It has **15 members**: **five permanent** members (the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China), each with a **veto**, and **ten non-permanent** members elected by the General Assembly for **two-year terms**.

marking_scheme.step: Ten non-permanent members, two-year terms, elected by the Assembly

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the General Assembly and the Security Council on three bases.
questions.solution_md: Three clear bases (membership, voting, nature of decisions), each with both sides stated.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Membership:** the Assembly includes **all 193 members**; the Council has only **15**.
2. **Voting:** the Assembly follows **one state, one vote**; in the Council the **five permanent members hold a veto** on substantive matters.
3. **Powers:** Assembly resolutions are mostly **recommendations**, while Council decisions on **peace and security** are the ones members have agreed to carry out.

marking_scheme.step: Nature of decisions or powers compared

questions.stem_md: What are the specialised agencies of the UN? Explain the work of any two of them.
questions.solution_md: A definition plus two agencies with their fields (WHO, ILO, FAO, UNESCO and similar are all acceptable).

answer.model_answer_md:
**Specialised agencies** are separate organisations linked to the UN through agreements, each working in one field and coordinated through **ECOSOC**.
- The **World Health Organization** sets health standards, fights epidemics and supports vaccination.
- The **International Labour Organization** sets standards for **workers' rights, working hours and safety**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the role of any five principal organs of the United Nations.
questions.solution_md: Five organs, one clear role each; naming the Trusteeship Council with its suspended status is also acceptable as one organ.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **General Assembly:** all member states meet, each with **one vote**; it discusses world issues, approves the budget and elects non-permanent Council members.
2. **Security Council:** **15 members**, five permanent with a **veto**; it has primary responsibility for **peace and security** and can authorise sanctions or peacekeeping.
3. **Economic and Social Council:** coordinates economic, social, health and educational work with the **specialised agencies**.
4. **International Court of Justice:** at **The Hague**, settles **legal disputes between states** and gives advisory opinions.
5. **Secretariat:** headed by the **Secretary-General**, carries out the daily **administration** of the UN. (The **Trusteeship Council** has been inactive since 1994.)

questions.stem_md: It is sometimes said that the UN has failed because wars still take place. Evaluate this view, giving points on both sides.
questions.solution_md: Two limits, two achievements and a reasoned conclusion; any balanced judgement with reasons earns the last mark.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Limits:**
1. The **veto** lets one permanent member block action, so the Council sometimes **cannot respond** to a crisis.
2. The UN has **no army of its own**; it depends on members for troops, money and will.
**Achievements:**
3. It gives every state a **forum to talk**, which has helped cool many disputes before they became wars.
4. **Peacekeeping**, help for **refugees**, disease control and food aid have saved many lives.
5. **Conclusion:** the UN cannot stop every war, but the world would likely be **less safe without it**; reform can make it more effective.

questions.stem_md: The debate on reforming the UN after the Cold War has two broad parts. They are reform of

options.text_md: the UN flag and the UN anthem
the organisation's structures and processes, and a review of the issues that fall within its jurisdiction
the national constitutions of member states, and their election laws
the location of the headquarters, and the official languages only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the organisation's structures and processes, and a review of the issues that fall within its jurisdiction. Reform is discussed under two heads: structures and processes (for example, the make-up of the Security Council) and jurisdiction (which issues the UN should deal with). The other options are not part of this debate.

questions.stem_md: Which change in the world since 1945 is most often given as a reason for changing the membership of the Security Council?

options.text_md: The UN has moved its headquarters out of New York
The General Assembly has stopped meeting
All the permanent members have given up their veto
The number of UN members has grown greatly, with many new states from Asia, Africa and Latin America, while the permanent five are unchanged

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The number of UN members has grown greatly, with many new states from Asia, Africa and Latin America, while the permanent five are unchanged. Membership grew from 51 to 193, mostly through newly independent states, but the permanent five reflect the world of 1945. The other statements are untrue.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following has NOT been commonly proposed as a criterion for a new permanent member of the Security Council?

options.text_md: Being the country with the highest number of tourists
Being a major economic power
Contributing substantially to the UN budget
Respecting democracy and human rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Being the country with the highest number of tourists. Proposals in the reform debate include economic and military weight, budget contribution, population, respect for democracy and human rights, and representation of the world's regions. Tourist numbers have never been a criterion.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is commonly put forward in support of India's claim to a permanent seat on the Security Council?

options.text_md: India is the only country that has never sent troops abroad
India was the first country to sign the Atlantic Charter
India has long taken part in UN peacekeeping missions and is one of the world's largest democracies
India has the smallest population in Asia

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** India has long taken part in UN peacekeeping missions and is one of the world's largest democracies. Arguments made for India include its large population and democracy, its long role in peacekeeping, its growing economy and its regular contributions to the UN. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: In the debate on Security Council reform, some states oppose adding any new permanent members at all. Which reason is most consistent with their position?

options.text_md: They believe the Council should have no members
They want the General Assembly to be abolished
They fear that more permanent seats, especially with a veto, would make the Council even less democratic
They think the UN should stop dealing with peace and security

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They fear that more permanent seats, especially with a veto, would make the Council even less democratic. Opponents of new permanent seats often argue that adding privileged members would widen inequality; some prefer more elected seats instead. The other options do not describe a real position in the debate.

questions.stem_md: India has worked with which group of countries, each seeking a permanent seat, to press for Security Council reform?

options.text_md: Brazil, Germany and Japan
Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka
France, the UK and the USA
Canada, Mexico and Australia

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Brazil, Germany and Japan. India, Brazil, Germany and Japan (the G4) support each other's claims to permanent seats. France, the UK and the USA already hold permanent seats, and the other groups are not reform blocs of this kind.

questions.stem_md: After the Cold War, some observers worried that the UN could be influenced too much by a single dominant power. Which feature of the UN is most relevant to that worry?

options.text_md: Every member has one vote in the General Assembly
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague
The UN has six official languages
The largest contributor to the budget and a veto-holding member can shape what the organisation does or does not do

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The largest contributor to the budget and a veto-holding member can shape what the organisation does or does not do. Budget dependence and the veto give a powerful member leverage over the UN's agenda. Equal voting in the Assembly works the other way, and the ICJ's location and the official languages are unrelated.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many states argue that the Security Council no longer represents the world of today.

**Reason (R):** Its permanent members were fixed in 1945, while the UN's membership has since grown to include many states from Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the gap between the 1945 permanent five and today's much larger and more diverse membership is the main basis of the complaint.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India has served as a non-permanent member of the Security Council more than once.

**Reason (R):** India has held a permanent seat with a veto since 1945.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: India has been elected to the Council several times. R is false: India is not a permanent member and has no veto; a permanent seat is exactly what it seeks.

questions.stem_md: True or false? All UN members agree that the veto power of the permanent members should be abolished immediately.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Opinion is divided: many states criticise the veto, some want it limited, and the permanent members themselves oppose giving it up; changing the Charter also needs their agreement.

questions.stem_md: The two broad areas of UN reform are reform of its structures and ___, and a review of the issues within its ___.
questions.solution_md: Reform covers structures and processes on one side and jurisdiction (the issues it deals with) on the other.

questions.stem_md: What are the two kinds of reform being discussed for the United Nations?
questions.solution_md: Name both kinds and give an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Reform of **structures and processes**, for example changing the **membership and voting** of the Security Council.
2. A **review of jurisdiction**, that is, deciding which **issues** (such as terrorism or development) the UN should handle.

marking_scheme.step: Structures and processes with an example

questions.stem_md: Give one argument for keeping the veto power and one argument against it.
questions.solution_md: One reasoned argument on each side.

answer.model_answer_md:
**For:** the veto keeps the **major powers inside** the UN, because they know no decision can be forced on them, so the organisation does not collapse as the League did.
**Against:** it lets **one state block action** wanted by most members, which is **undemocratic** and can leave the Council silent in a crisis.

questions.stem_md: State three arguments that India puts forward in support of its claim to a permanent seat in the Security Council.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct arguments: population and democracy, peacekeeping record, economic weight and conduct.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. India is one of the **two most populous** countries and the **largest democracy**, so its inclusion would make the Council more representative.
2. It has been one of the **biggest contributors of troops** to UN **peacekeeping** for decades.
3. It is a **large and growing economy**, pays its UN dues regularly and has followed a policy of **peaceful dispute settlement**.

questions.stem_md: Mention any three criteria that have been proposed for admitting new permanent members to the Security Council.
questions.solution_md: Any three of the commonly proposed criteria.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Being a **major economic power** and, in some proposals, a **major military power**.
2. Making a **substantial contribution to the UN budget**.
3. Having a **large population**, **respecting democracy and human rights**, and making the Council **more representative** of the world's regions and cultures. (Any three.)

questions.stem_md: Should the Security Council be expanded by adding new permanent members? Present arguments on both sides and give your reasoned view.
questions.solution_md: Two points for, two against and a reasoned personal conclusion; the conclusion is marked for reasoning, not for which side is chosen.

answer.model_answer_md:
**In favour:**
1. The Council reflects **1945**, not today; regions such as **Africa and Latin America** have no permanent seat.
2. Adding major states with large populations and economies would make its decisions **more legitimate** and easier to enforce.
**Against:**
3. More permanent seats, especially with a **veto**, could make the Council **slower** and more often blocked.
4. It may create a **new privileged group** and leave smaller states with even less voice; some prefer more **elected** seats instead.
5. **Reasoned view:** expansion is needed for **representation**, but it works best with limits on the veto and a fair regional balance (any balanced, reasoned view earns this mark).

questions.stem_md: Explain India's position on the reform of the United Nations and the objections that have been raised to its claim for a permanent seat.
questions.solution_md: Three points on India's position and claim, two on objections; stated neutrally as the views of different states.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. India supports a **stronger and more democratic UN** and wants the Security Council to be **more representative** of developing countries.
2. It argues for **more members**, both permanent and non-permanent, so that the Council reflects the present world.
3. It points to its **population, democracy, economy** and long **peacekeeping** record in support of its own claim, and works with **Brazil, Germany and Japan** for this.
4. **Objections** raised by some states include India's **nuclear weapons**, its **disputes with neighbours**, and doubts about whether it can represent its whole region.
5. Other states, including some neighbours, prefer **no new permanent seats** at all, which makes the reform hard to achieve.

marking_scheme.step: India's view of a more representative UN

questions.stem_md: Which international organisation oversees the international financial system and gives advice and loans to countries facing balance of payments problems?

options.text_md: The World Trade Organization
The International Monetary Fund
Human Rights Watch
The International Atomic Energy Agency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The International Monetary Fund. The IMF watches over the global monetary and financial system and lends to members in payments difficulty. The WTO deals with trade rules, Human Rights Watch is a human rights NGO, and the IAEA deals with nuclear energy.

questions.stem_md: An imagined developing country, Nilgaon, needs a long-term loan to build rural roads and improve its schools. Which organisation is it most likely to approach?

options.text_md: The World Bank
Amnesty International
The International Court of Justice
The IAEA

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The World Bank. The World Bank gives loans and grants for development projects such as infrastructure, education and health. Amnesty is a human rights NGO, the ICJ is a court and the IAEA deals with nuclear matters.

questions.stem_md: An imagined country, Kanakdesh, complains that another member has raised import duties on its textiles in breach of agreed trade rules. Which organisation provides the rules and the dispute process for such a complaint?

options.text_md: The International Labour Organization
The World Trade Organization
The Trusteeship Council
Human Rights Watch

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The World Trade Organization. The WTO sets the rules of international trade and has a system for settling trade disputes between members. The other bodies deal with labour, trust territories and human rights.

questions.stem_md: The International Atomic Energy Agency was set up in 1957 mainly to

options.text_md: build nuclear weapons for the permanent members
regulate world trade in textiles
promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevent its use for military purposes
run elections in newly independent countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevent its use for military purposes. The IAEA promotes peaceful nuclear technology and, through inspections, tries to ensure it is not diverted to weapons. It does not build weapons, regulate textiles or run elections.

questions.stem_md: Amnesty International is best described as

options.text_md: a specialised agency of the UN whose decisions are binding on all governments
a military alliance of democratic states
a bank that lends to poor countries
a non-governmental organisation that campaigns for human rights and publishes reports on their violation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a non-governmental organisation that campaigns for human rights and publishes reports on their violation. Amnesty is an NGO: it researches abuses, publishes reports and campaigns; it has no power to bind governments. It is not a UN agency, an alliance or a bank.

questions.stem_md: An NGO based in New York researches abuses such as the use of child soldiers and landmines, draws media attention to them and lobbies governments to change policy. This most closely describes the work of

options.text_md: the World Bank
the IMF
the Security Council
Human Rights Watch

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Human Rights Watch. Human Rights Watch is an international NGO that investigates and publicises human rights abuses and campaigns for change; it helped build campaigns against landmines and the use of child soldiers. The others are inter-governmental bodies with different roles.

questions.stem_md: The IMF and the World Bank were planned at a conference held in 1944 at

options.text_md: San Francisco
Geneva
Bretton Woods
The Hague

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Bretton Woods. Both institutions were planned at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944 and are therefore called the Bretton Woods institutions. The UN Charter was signed at San Francisco.

questions.stem_md: Critics argue that developing countries have less say in the IMF than their numbers suggest. Which feature of the IMF is the main basis of this criticism?

options.text_md: Each member has exactly one vote
Voting power is weighted by each member's financial contribution (quota), so the richest members hold a large share of votes
Only developing countries can borrow from it
It is run by NGOs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Voting power is weighted by each member's financial contribution (quota), so the richest members hold a large share of votes. Votes in the IMF follow members' quotas, so a small number of rich countries carry a large share of the vote. One member, one vote is the General Assembly rule, and the other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Developing countries often complain that major economic powers have a strong influence on WTO negotiations.

**Reason (R):** The World Trade Organization was set up in 1995 as the successor to the GATT framework.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. The complaint arises from the bargaining strength of large economies, not from the date the WTO was set up; so R, though true, does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human rights NGOs such as Amnesty International can influence governments even though they have no power to enforce decisions.

**Reason (R):** Their reports draw public and media attention to abuses, which puts pressure on governments to act.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the influence of such NGOs comes from information and publicity, not from legal power.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are principal organs of the United Nations.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Both are non-governmental organisations, independent of governments; the six principal organs are the Assembly, the Security Council, ECOSOC, the ICJ, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council.

questions.stem_md: Match each organisation outside the six principal organs with the field it works in.

options.text_md: International Monetary Fund
World Bank
World Trade Organization
International Atomic Energy Agency

match_right.text_md: Peaceful use of nuclear energy and safeguards
Loans and grants for development projects
Global financial system and help with payments crises

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). IMF: finance and payments; World Bank: development; WTO: trade rules; IAEA: nuclear energy.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the role of the IMF and that of the World Bank.
questions.solution_md: One clear role for each, showing the contrast between financial stability and development.

answer.model_answer_md: The **IMF** looks after the stability of the **international financial system**, advises on economic policy and lends to countries facing **balance of payments** crises. The **World Bank** gives **loans and grants for development**, such as roads, schools, health and farming.

questions.stem_md: Why was the International Atomic Energy Agency set up? Mention two of its functions.
questions.solution_md: Purpose plus two functions: promotion of peaceful uses and safeguard inspections.

answer.model_answer_md:
It was set up in **1957** to promote the **peaceful use of nuclear energy**.
1. It helps countries use nuclear technology for **power, medicine and farming**.
2. Its **inspectors** check that nuclear facilities are **not used for weapons**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state, Sarovar, detains journalists without trial. Explain two ways in which an NGO such as Amnesty International may respond.
questions.solution_md: Two NGO methods: research and reports, and campaigns or pressure; NGOs cannot enforce decisions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It may **investigate and publish a report** on the detentions, drawing **media and public attention** to them.
2. It may run **campaigns and appeals**, urging people and other governments to press Sarovar to **release or fairly try** the journalists.

questions.stem_md: What is the World Trade Organization? Why do some developing countries criticise the way it works?
questions.solution_md: A definition with its origin, then two criticisms from developing countries.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **WTO**, set up in **1995** as the successor to **GATT**, sets the **rules for global trade** and settles trade disputes among its members.
Criticisms:
